doc.title: Mat Domber interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2007

title: Smoky clubs, low pay and the mob
summary: Davern loved smoky clubs; Domber says mobsters owned clubs and hired jazz musicians.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: They always worked the thirty dollar gigs, or at that time the thirty-five dollar gigs in places, you know, in the smoky bars. But they had a certain joy of doing it. Kenny Davern used to tell me that he loved the smoke, he loved the atmosphere of the clubs and the bars, you know, thick with smoke and booze and all of that stuff. And that was where jazz was born and that was really the atmosphere in which jazz was created. We’ve lost a lot of that because you can’t smoke anymore.

Most of the people from those days are on AA or worse. It’s different. Of course we also had — somebody should write a book someplace, sometime, about the influence of the mob on jazz. You know it was the mobsters who owned most of the clubs. It was the mobsters who, in Chicago and New York, who hired the jazz musicians who somehow or other liked jazz themselves and used it in the speakeasies and in the clubs etcetera, and that opened up a whole world. Maybe they still do but more respectably, I don’t know.
